description: Transverse and longitudinal waves, wave properties, and the wave speed equation v = fλ.
content_html:
Types of Wave

Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. The particles of the medium vibrate about their rest positions but do not travel along with the wave. There are two fundamental categories:

• Transverse waves — the vibrations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. The wave profile forms crests and troughs. All electromagnetic waves, water surface ripples and waves on a string are transverse.
• Longitudinal waves — the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Instead of crests and troughs, these waves have compressions (particles close together) and rarefactions (particles spread apart). Sound is the principal example at GCSE.

A critical distinction: mechanical waves such as sound and water waves require a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel through. Electromagnetic waves such as light require no medium and can travel through a vacuum.

Key Fact

Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Transverse: vibrations perpendicular to travel direction (crests and troughs). Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to travel direction (compressions and rarefactions). Sound is mechanical — it needs a medium.

Wave Properties

All waves — transverse and longitudinal — are described using four measurable properties:

• Amplitude — the maximum displacement from the rest position, measured in metres (m). A larger amplitude means more energy carried: louder sound, brighter light.

• Wavelength (\(\lambda\)) — the distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest), measured in metres.

• Frequency (\(f\)) — the number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency means higher pitch for sound, or higher energy for light.

• Period (\(T\)) — the time taken for one complete wave to pass a fixed point, measured in seconds. Period and frequency are reciprocals of each other: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\). A wave with a frequency of 200 Hz has a period of \(\frac{1}{200} = 0.005\) s.

The Wave Speed Equation

Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are related by the wave equation:

$$v = f \times \lambda$$

where \(v\) is wave speed in m/s, \(f\) is frequency in Hz, and \(\lambda\) is wavelength in m. Rearranging: \(f = \frac{v}{\lambda}\) and \(\lambda = \frac{v}{f}\). This equation applies to all waves — mechanical and electromagnetic alike.

Question: A sound wave travels through air with a frequency of 440 Hz and a wavelength of 0.77 m. Calculate the wave speed.

Step 1 — identify values: \(f = 440\) Hz, \(\lambda = 0.77\) m.

Step 2 — apply equation: \(v = f \times \lambda = 440 \times 0.77 = 339\) m/s.

Step 3 — state units: wave speed = 339 m/s (close to the speed of sound in air at room temperature — a good sense check).

Reflection, Refraction and Diffraction

Waves interact with surfaces and boundaries in three important ways:

• Reflection — a wave bounces back from a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal). Wave speed, frequency and wavelength do not change.

• Refraction — a wave changes speed when it crosses a boundary between two media (e.g. air into glass). If it hits at an angle, it also changes direction. It bends towards the normal when slowing down and away from the normal when speeding up. Frequency stays the same; wavelength changes.

• Diffraction — a wave spreads out after passing through a gap or around the edge of an obstacle. The effect is greatest when the gap width is similar in size to the wavelength. Wider gaps produce less spreading.

Key Fact

Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Refraction: wave changes speed (and direction) at a boundary — bends towards the normal when slowing down. Diffraction: wave spreads through a gap most when gap width ≈ wavelength.

In a ripple tank, a vibrating bar produces plane water waves. A light source above projects the wave pattern onto a screen below. To measure wave speed: use a strobe light to “freeze” the pattern, measure several wavelengths and divide by the number of waves to find \(\lambda\). Note the motor frequency for \(f\). Calculate \(v = f\lambda\).

For investigating wave speed in a stretched string (PAG P11): vary the tension by changing the hanging mass, measure the frequency using a signal generator driving the string, and observe the standing wave pattern to determine wavelength from the node spacing. Increasing tension increases wave speed.

Key variables to control: for the string, keep the length and mass per unit length constant when changing tension. For the ripple tank, keep water depth constant — wave speed in water depends on depth.

The speed of sound in a medium depends on the stiffness and density of the material. Sound travels faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases, because particles in solids are more tightly bonded and can transmit compressions more rapidly. For example, sound travels at approximately 340 m/s in air but around 1,500 m/s in water and over 5,000 m/s in steel.
exam_tip_html: When answering wave equation questions, always write out the formula \(v = f \times \lambda\) before substituting values, and include units at every step. A common error is failing to convert between Hz and kHz, or between nm and m — check units carefully before calculating. For describe or explain questions about refraction, remember to mention whether the wave speeds up or slows down AND which way it bends relative to the normal. Diffraction questions often ask about the conditions for maximum spreading — the gap width must be similar to the wavelength.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Transverse waves vibrate perpendicular to their travel direction (e.g. EM waves); longitudinal waves vibrate parallel (e.g. sound), with compressions and rarefactions.
  • Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by \(v = f\lambda\). Rearrange as needed, always check units.
  • At boundaries, waves reflect (equal angles), refract (change speed and direction) or diffract (spread through gaps — greatest effect when gap ≈ wavelength).

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a longitudinal wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a wave in which the vibrations/oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer/wave travel.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a compression and a rarefaction in a sound wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a compression is a region where particles are pushed close together (high pressure). 1 mark: a rarefaction is a region where particles are spread further apart (low pressure).

practice_questions.text: A water wave has a frequency of 2.5 Hz and a wavelength of 0.4 m. Calculate the wave speed. Show your working and give the unit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct equation v = f × λ. 1 mark: correct substitution v = 2.5 × 0.4. 1 mark: correct answer 1.0. 1 mark: correct unit m/s.

practice_questions.text: Explain why sound diffracts around a doorway but visible light does not.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that diffraction is greatest when gap width is similar to wavelength; states that sound has wavelengths similar in size to a doorway (tens of centimetres) whereas visible light has a much shorter wavelength (hundreds of nanometres), so light shows negligible diffraction through a doorway. Secure: states sound diffracts because its wavelength is similar to the gap; light does not because its wavelength is much smaller than the gap. Developing: states that the wavelength of sound is similar to the doorway but does not quantify or compare light's wavelength. Emerging: vague reference to wavelength without a comparison.

practice_questions.text: A wave travels from air into glass and bends towards the normal. What does this tell you about the wave's speed in glass compared to air?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: The wave slows down in glass. Distractors: The wave speeds up in glass; The wave's frequency decreases; The wave's amplitude increases.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a ripple tank is a suitable method for measuring the speed of water waves. Include limitations in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: describes method clearly (measure λ from wave pattern, record frequency from motor, apply v = fλ); evaluates limitations (parallax error reading wavelength from screen, water depth affects speed so must be kept constant, waves may not be perfectly planar near edges); concludes it is suitable with care. Secure: describes method and identifies at least two limitations. Developing: describes basic method but limitations are vague. Emerging: mentions ripple tank without explaining how measurements are taken.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of wave has vibrations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer?
A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6 m. What is its speed?
Diffraction is greatest when the gap width is _____ to the wavelength of the wave.
When a wave enters a denser medium and slows down, it bends _____ the normal.
Match each wave property to its definition.

flashcard_questions.a: A wave where vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
A wave where vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the SI unit of frequency?
In the wave equation v = fλ, what does λ represent?
flashcard_questions.a: Wavelength — the distance from one crest to the next.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the amplitude of a wave?
flashcard_questions.a: The maximum displacement of a particle from its rest (equilibrium) position.

flashcard_questions.q: A sound wave has f = 340 Hz and λ = 1 m. What is its speed?
What are the regions of high and low pressure in a sound wave called?
When a wave bends towards the normal at a boundary, what happens to its speed?

flashcard_questions.a: The spreading of a wave after passing through a gap or around an obstacle.
When the gap width is similar in size to the wavelength.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does sound but not visible light diffract around doorways?
flashcard_questions.a: Sound's wavelength is similar to doorway width; light's wavelength is far smaller.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the frequency of a wave when it refracts?
flashcard_questions.a: Frequency stays the same — only speed and wavelength change.

glossary_terms.definition: A wave in which the vibrations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer.
A wave in which the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are pushed close together, creating a higher-pressure zone.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread further apart, creating a lower-pressure zone.
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its equilibrium (rest) position; related to the energy carried by the wave.
The distance between two equivalent adjacent points on a wave, such as crest to crest or compression to compression.
The number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
An imaginary line perpendicular to a surface at the point where a wave meets it; angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal.
